items.prompt: Explain how a mining function can cause a settlement to grow and later decline.
items.canonical_answer: The discovery of a mineral such as diamonds is the factor that creates mining jobs, which attract migrants, and their spending supports shops and services, so the settlement grows. When the deposit is worked out or richer deposits are found elsewhere, mining stops, jobs are lost and people leave, so the settlement declines, as Kolmanskop did after 1928 until it was abandoned in 1956.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: a mineral discovery creating mining jobs.
1 mark for the link: jobs attract migrants because of work and income, supporting services.
1 mark for the result: the end of mining causes job losses.
1 mark for the effect of out-migration and decline, with an example such as Kolmanskop.

items.prompt: Area X has twelve-storey blocks of flats where 40% of households lack piped water. Area Y has single-storey houses where 98% of households have piped water. Explain the error in concluding that Area X has the higher quality of life because its buildings are taller. What evidence discriminates between the areas?
items.canonical_answer: The error is the confusion of building height with living conditions: height describes the form of buildings, not the wellbeing of the people living in them. The correct distinction uses service and household indicators, and here the piped-water data point the other way, showing better conditions in Area Y. The test is to compare indicators such as access to water, sanitation, overcrowding and income rather than the number of storeys.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the confusion/error of using height as a measure of quality of life.
1 mark for the correct distinction using the piped-water data, with a test based on living-condition indicators.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that building a ring road is the best way to reduce traffic congestion in a CBD?
items.canonical_answer: Partly agree. A ring road diverts through-traffic that does not need to enter the centre, so fewer vehicles use the narrow CBD streets and lorries can avoid the centre. However, it does nothing for the many people who travel into the CBD to work and shop, it is expensive and takes land, and new roads can attract more traffic. Measures aimed at CBD-bound traffic, such as better public transport, park-and-ride, bus lanes, pedestrianised streets and restrictions on large vehicles, are also needed. A ring road helps most where through-traffic is a large share of the congestion, but it is best combined with these measures.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for evidence of how a ring road reduces congestion.
Up to 2 C marks for limitations with reasons, or alternative measures for CBD-bound traffic.
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

items.prompt:
(a) Name the rural pattern of a compact dwelling cluster. [1]
(b) Describe three distinct influences on rural settlement sites or arrangement. [3]
(c) Name the measure describing a rising proportion living in urban areas. [1]
(d) Describe the urban change: 400 of 1,000 residents urban before; 600 of 1,200 after, with compatible definitions. [2]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Nucleated. (b) Any three, e.g.: flat, gently sloping land is easier to build on, so homes concentrate there; a reliable water supply such as a river or borehole attracts homes; fertile soil supports farming, so people settle near their fields; roads make it easier to reach markets and services, so homes line up along them; government planning or land allocation decides where villages may be built. (c) Urbanisation. (d) Urban count rises 200 while its share rises from 40% to 50%; both urban growth and urbanisation occur.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for nucleated.
(b) 3 A marks for three distinct settlement-factor point descriptions.
(c) 1 A mark for urbanisation.
(d) 2 B marks for the number and share interpretations.

items.prompt:
Two hypothetical housing locations have monthly housing/transport/service costs: A N$900/600/300; B N$1,000/200/200. The household has N$1,500 for these specified costs. Other expenses and housing quality are not supplied.
(a) Name the model of MEDC city structure in which zones form rings around the CBD. [1]
(b) Calculate B’s combined specified monthly cost. [2]
(c) Describe three distinct supported cost/budget comparisons. [3]
(d) What judgement is supported about the claim “B must be the better complete housing solution”? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) The concentric zone (Burgess) model. (b) 1,000+200+200 = N$1,400 per month. (c) A has a lower housing charge but higher combined total, N$1,800 versus N$1,400; A exceeds the specified budget by N$300; B is N$100 below it. Credit distinct comparisons without repeated credit for equivalent expressions of one total difference. (d) B fits the stated cost bundle better, but complete suitability is not established without other expenses, quality and access evidence.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for the concentric zone (Burgess) model.
(b) 2 B marks for the sum method and correct total with currency/period.
(c) 3 B marks for distinct resource-based comparison patterns and budget evidence.
(d) 1 C mark for a supported bounded suitability judgement.

items.prompt: Windhoek's Informal Settlement Upgrading Project supports affordable housing on serviced land. How far do you agree that upgrading informal settlements where they are is better than moving residents to new housing schemes elsewhere? [5]
items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Upgrading in place keeps people close to their jobs, schools, relatives and neighbours, so livelihoods and support networks are not broken, and adding water, toilets, roads and electricity to an existing area is usually cheaper than building whole new towns. Collaborative projects such as Windhoek's let residents help plan the work. However, some settlements are on land that floods or is too densely packed to service safely, so some families may need to move, and upgraded plots and loans must still be affordable for the poorest. Upgrading is generally the better approach, with relocation used only where a site is unsafe.
marking_guidance: Up to 3 C marks for evidence supporting upgrading in place (jobs, networks, cost, participation).
Up to 1 C mark for a reason relocation may be needed (flood risk, density) or for affordability limits.
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.
